papers.title: Different forms of autophagy restrict neurite outgrowth in disparate compartments in a single neuron
papers.summary: This paper investigates how different forms of autophagy control neurite outgrowth within distinct parts of a single neuron. The researchers likely found that specific autophagy pathways act locally, restricting growth in one compartment (such as axons or dendrites) while not affecting others, revealing compartment-specific regulation. This suggests neurons use spatially distinct autophagic machinery to fine-tune their morphology during development.
papers.why: Understanding how compartment-specific autophagy shapes neuronal structure directly informs the project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, offering mechanistic insight relevant to interneuron morphology and connectivity.

papers.title: Redox-exercise crosstalk in neurodegenerative diseases: mechanistic perspectives on antioxidant interactions with Nrf2-BDNF signaling, autophagy, and mitochondrial plasticity.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how physical exercise and antioxidants interact with the Nrf2-BDNF signaling pathway to influence oxidative stress responses in neurodegenerative diseases. It focuses on how these interventions affect autophagy processes and mitochondrial plasticity, which are key cellular mechanisms for clearing damaged components and maintaining energy production. The review likely synthesizes mechanistic evidence connecting redox balance, exercise-induced signaling, and neuroprotection.
papers.why: This review's focus on autophagy and mitochondrial plasticity mechanisms in neurodegenerative disease contexts is directly relevant to understanding mitophagy pathways in neurons, even though it lacks spatial or interneuron-specific data.

papers.title: Ginsenoside Rh1 Modulates GABAergic Inhibitory Homeostasis and Mitochondrial Quality Control During Lead (Pb)-Associated Neuronal Dysfunction.
papers.summary: This study examines how Ginsenoside Rh1, a natural plant compound, affects neurons exposed to lead (Pb) toxicity. It focuses on two systems: GABAergic signaling (the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter system) and mitochondrial quality control, which includes processes like mitophagy that clear damaged mitochondria. The findings suggest Rh1 may help restore balance to inhibitory neuron function and mitochondrial health disrupted by lead exposure.
papers.why: This paper directly connects to the project's core interests in mitophagy and GABAergic interneuron function in the context of neuronal stress, offering potential mechanistic insight applicable to broader neurodegeneration research.

papers.title: Translophagy-A potential link between autophagy impairment and translational errors.
papers.summary: This paper discusses 'translophagy,' a proposed connection between autophagy and errors that occur during protein translation. It suggests that when autophagy (the cell's waste-clearing system) is impaired, faulty or misfolded proteins from translational mistakes may accumulate and require specialized autophagic clearance. This concept links two quality-control systems in cells: the accuracy of protein synthesis and the cell's ability to degrade its own dysfunctional components.
papers.why: Understanding autophagy impairment as a driver of protein quality control failure is directly relevant to studying mitophagy and autophagy dysfunction in neurons, particularly in vulnerable interneuron populations.

papers.title: TEX264-mediated ER-phagy dysfunction contributes to Cadmium-induced ER stress: Implication of hippocampal neuronal apoptosis and cognitive deficits.
papers.summary: This study investigates how cadmium exposure disrupts TEX264-mediated ER-phagy, a selective autophagy process that clears damaged endoplasmic reticulum. The researchers show that this dysfunction leads to accumulation of ER stress in hippocampal neurons. This ER stress subsequently triggers neuronal apoptosis and results in measurable cognitive deficits, likely in an animal model.
papers.why: This paper offers relevant mechanistic insight into selective autophagy pathway dysfunction (ER-phagy) in hippocampal neurons, directly complementing the project's focus on mitophagy/autophagy dysregulation in neuronal populations, even though it centers on ER-phagy rather than mitophagy specifically.
papers.figure: A figure showing TEX264 expression/localization alongside ER stress markers and apoptosis staining in hippocampal tissue sections, ideally with quantification correlating ER-phagy flux to cognitive test outcomes.

papers.title: Propofol regulates SLC6A2 expression via NAT10-mediated ac4C modification to modulate excessive mitophagy and hippocampal neuron dysfunction in aged postoperative cognitive dysfunction.
papers.summary: This study looks at how the anesthetic propofol affects a gene called SLC6A2 in the brains of aged animals experiencing postoperative cognitive dysfunction (a decline in memory/thinking after surgery). The regulation happens through a chemical modification (ac4C) on RNA, controlled by an enzyme called NAT10. This process influences excessive mitophagy (breakdown of damaged mitochondria) in hippocampal neurons, which in turn affects neuron function and cognitive outcomes.
papers.why: This paper directly examines excessive mitophagy in hippocampal neurons and its molecular regulation, offering mechanistic insight relevant to neuronal mitophagy pathways central to the PhD project.

papers.title: Neuron-derived SPP1 instructs microglia to limit degeneration.
papers.summary: This paper likely shows that neurons release the protein SPP1 (osteopontin) as a signal to nearby microglia. This signal appears to instruct microglia to adopt a protective role that limits neurodegeneration. The study probably combines neuron-microglia interaction models with molecular and imaging approaches to demonstrate this signaling axis.
papers.why: Understanding neuron-microglia crosstalk via SPP1 in limiting degeneration is relevant to studying how neuronal stress signals (potentially linked to mitophagy/autophagy dysfunction) shape microglial responses in the brain, which could intersect with spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic profiling of interneuron microenvironments.

papers.title: Intranasal Administration of Insulin and IGF-1 Protects Hippocampal CA1 Neurons Against Transient Global Forebrain Ischemia by Inhibiting Autophagy, Apoptosis and Neuroinflammation: A Comparative Study.
papers.summary: This study tests whether giving insulin or IGF-1 through the nose can protect hippocampal CA1 neurons from damage caused by temporarily cutting off blood flow to the brain (global forebrain ischemia). The researchers compared the two treatments and found both reduced harmful autophagy, programmed cell death (apoptosis), and inflammation in the brain. The work suggests intranasal insulin/IGF-1 could be a neuroprotective strategy against ischemic neuronal injury.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it examines autophagy regulation in neurons during brain injury, directly connecting to the project's focus on mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms in neuronal survival, even though it lacks spatial transcriptomic or interneuron-specific analysis.
